concept_card.core_rule: A simple random sample gives each population member an equal chance of selection, ensuring independent trials. For simple random samples of size $n$ from a large population (or independent Bernoulli trials with constant parameter $p$), the sample proportion $\hat{p}=X/n$ has expected value $\text{E}(\hat{p})=p$ and standard deviation $\text{SD}(\hat{p})=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$; when $np\ge10$ and $n(1-p)\ge10$, its distribution is approximately normal by the Central Limit Theorem.

hint_levels.template: Check how the sample was selected before calculating: randomness protects against bias, and $\hat{p}$ varies around $p$.
Compute $\hat{p}=\frac{\text{successes}}{n}$, then use mean $p$ and sd $\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$; use $\hat p$ only as an estimate when $p$ is unknown.
Repeated samples are dart throws at the population target: a fair random process clusters around $p$, while a biased process aims off-centre.

explanation_sections.heading: Random samples and bias
explanation_sections.body: A random sample selects population members by a chance mechanism so each has a known, non-zero chance of selection. Avoid convenience, voluntary-response and under-coverage bias; use a random-number generator, shuffled list or systematic procedure with a random start, and record the population and sampling frame.

explanation_sections.heading: Sample proportion
explanation_sections.body: $\hat{p}=\frac{X}{n}$ where $X$ is the number of successes in a sample of size $n$. It is a random variable across repeated samples and a point estimate of the population proportion $p$ for one observed sample.

explanation_sections.heading: Sampling distribution
explanation_sections.body: Across many random samples, $E(\hat p)=p$ and $\mathrm{SD}(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$. The distribution is approximately normal when $np\ge10$ and $n(1-p)\ge10$; larger $n$ reduces the spread.

explanation_sections.heading: Repeated sampling and standardisation
explanation_sections.body: Use technology to simulate repeated samples and plot the resulting proportions. Compare the centre and spread with the normal model, and examine the approximately standard normal statistic $\frac{\hat p-p}{\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}}$ (or the estimated version using $\hat p$ in the denominator). Comment on how $n$ and $p$ affect the approximation.

explanation_sections.heading: Graphical checks
explanation_sections.body: Read dot plots, histograms and comparative displays of real or simulated samples drawn from uniform, Bernoulli, binomial and normal populations. Check the scale, centre, spread, shape and outliers. Sampling distributions can be approximately normal even when the underlying Bernoulli data contain only zeros and ones.

concept_card.core_rule: An interval estimate uses a sample proportion to give plausible values for the population proportion: $\hat{p}\pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$. The margin of error is $z\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$; higher confidence widens it, larger samples narrow it, and repeated samples produce varying intervals, most but not all of which contain the true $p$.

explanation_sections.heading: Interval estimates and conditions
explanation_sections.body: For a proportion, use $\hat{p}\pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$. The approximation requires a random or otherwise defensible sample, approximate independence, and enough observed successes and failures for the normal approximation. For sampling without replacement, also check that the sample is a small fraction of the population.

explanation_sections.heading: Margin of error and interpretation
explanation_sections.body: The margin of error is $z\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}$. It shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$ and grows with higher confidence. '95% confident' describes the long-run method: if random sampling and interval construction were repeated, about 95% of intervals would contain the true $p$.

explanation_sections.heading: Confidence, sample size and variation
explanation_sections.body: Increasing confidence increases $z$ and widens the interval; increasing $n$ decreases the standard error and narrows it at the rate $1/\sqrt n$. Different random samples give different $\hat p$ values and endpoints, so most — but not all — intervals from a 95% method contain $p$.

explanation_sections.heading: Common interpretation trap
explanation_sections.body: A 95% confidence interval does not mean there is a 95% probability that the specific interval contains $p$; rather, it describes the reliability of the estimation process.

explanation_sections.heading: Technology and reasonableness
explanation_sections.body: Use a calculator, spreadsheet or statistical tool to obtain $z$, standard errors, endpoints and sample-size requirements. Check the sampling assumptions, retain sufficient precision and interpret the interval on the proportion or percentage scale. An endpoint outside $[0,1]$ is a warning that this simple normal approximation may be unsuitable; do not silently clip it without explanation.

Constructing an interval without checking random sampling, independence and the large-count approximation.
